A Tuesday morning in mid-December, in the flat in Cotroceni. After almost two weeks in Bucharest, Mrs Suzuki and Mrs Fumiko are going back to Madrid today. Mihai has taken the day off to see them off at the airport. The taxi comes at nine. Mihai and Ana speak keigo with the sisters “for the last time”, and Ana has made the morning tea herself, for the first time.
Good morning. Were you able to sleep well last night?
Yes, thank you. Today we say goodbye to this room too.
This morning I made the tea. Please, help yourselves.
Oh, Ana made it? Then, thank you, I will. …Oh my, it’s good.
Really? I made it exactly as your card says.
The more often you make it, the better it gets. I’m sure it won’t take you fifty years.
The taxi comes at nine. Allow me to take you to the airport. I’ll carry your luggage.
Thank you. …Before that, there’s something I want to give you both.
Finally. It was so hard for me to keep quiet all this time.
(Holding out a box) Ana, please open it.
(Opening the box) Oh…! A tiny kimono!
It’s a garment for the newborn. Fumiko sewed it from our mother’s kimono.
From your mother’s kimono…! Is it really all right for us to accept something so precious?
Yes. The white hairpin Ana wore at the wedding was also our mother’s. I’m sure Mother is happy too.
And this is an amulet from the temple next to my teahouse. So that the baby is born healthy.
(Crying) Thank you so much. …The more I look at it, the more the tears come.
There’s one more thing. Please take a look at this.
An invitation…? May I read it? …“Celebration of the teahouse’s fiftieth anniversary”?
Yes. In the spring two years from now, my teahouse turns exactly fifty.
I’ve never once seen Fumiko’s teahouse. So on that day I’m definitely going.
Mihai, Ana, could you possibly come with the baby? I would love you to let me make the baby’s first tea with that cherry-wood spoon.
We’ll come with pleasure. …Only, allow me to say one thing as a doctor: the baby gets just one sip of tea.
The spring two years from now… The baby will already be over a year old.
Yes. We’ll be waiting for you in Kyoto, in cherry-blossom season.
(Looking out of the window) The more we see each other, the harder it is to say goodbye.
…Ah, the taxi has arrived. Well then, let’s go.

o-ma-chi shi-te o-ri-ma-su: the phrase is said smoothly, without a pause, with the pitch gently falling towards the end. Japanese people say it more softly and slowly than ordinary speech: you can hear politeness in the rhythm too.
go-ju(t)-shuu-nen: after “ju” comes a tiny stop (っ), then a long “shuu”. Don’t say “gojuushuunen”: っ doubles the consonant, like a held breath.
ma-i-ri-ma-su: “ai” is a double syllable — you hear both vowels. In まいりましょう, the “sho” at the end is long: ma-i-ri-ma-shoo.
1. 尊敬語: you raise the other person (ch. 36)

When you talk about what a respected person does (a guest, a client, someone much older), you raise THEIR verb. The most common verbs have special words; for the rest there is the regular form お + stem + に なる.
きょうと に いらっしゃる (is in Kyoto)

Watch the last form: おやすみに なれました か puts the respectful verb おやすみに なる into the POTENTIAL (なれる = can become): “were you able to sleep well?”. It’s the classic question of a Japanese host in the morning. The third way, the passive as respect (いかれる, こられる), is easier but less polite.
Never 尊敬語 for yourself! Remember Mihai’s mistake in chapter 36: ひとり で おべんきょう に なりました (“I graciously deigned to study on my own”). For yourself: べんきょう しました or, humbly, べんきょう いたしました.
For what YOU (or your group) do towards the respected person, you lower your own verb. Special verbs + the regular form お + stem + する (ご + noun + する with Sino-Japanese verbs).
おまち して おります is doubly humble: お～する (I do it for you) + ～て おります (the humble form of ～て います). It’s the closing formula of every Japanese invitation: “we (humbly) await you”.

まいる is also used as neutral politeness for things: タクシー が まいりました (the taxi has arrived), でんしゃ が まいります. Mihai isn’t “lowering himself” before the taxi, he’s just speaking nicely. And don’t forget うち と そと: about your own boss, to a client, you still use 謙譲語 (イオネスク は もうして おりました).
The reverse trap: はいけん して ください (“please lower yourself and look”) is wrong, because はいけん is for you. For the other person: ごらん ください. Exactly Mihai’s mistake at the dinner with Mr Tanaka.

When you ask a respected person for something, you have three tools. お～ください (a respectful but firm request: oake kudasai), ～て いただけません か (a gentle question: “could I receive the favour of…?”) and ～させて いただく (you ask permission for an action of YOUR OWN).
Please take a look at this.
Could you possibly come with us?
Allow me to take you to the airport.
I’d like you to let me make the tea.

The ladder of requests, from simple to very polite: ～て ください → ～て くださいません か → ～て いただけません か → ～て いただけない でしょう か. The higher you climb, the more the request sounds like a question and leaves the other person free to say no.
Mihai uses ～させて いただく jokingly: いしゃ と して ひとこと いわせて いただきます (“allow me to say a word, as a doctor”). In English too, “allow me to…” often introduces a firm opinion, put nicely.
4. ～ば ～ほど and ほど, once more (ch. 39)
The farewell in the dialogue is full of “the more…, the more…”. The formula: the verb in ～ば + the same verb in dictionary form + ほど. For い-adjectives: ～ければ ～い ほど; for な-adjectives: ～なら ～な ほど.
The more often you make it, the better it gets.
The more I look at it, the more the tears come.
It’s not as good as Mrs Fumiko’s, but it’s good. (A は B ほど ～ない)
The verb あう is a godan verb ending in う: its ～ば form is あえば (not “あうば”). Likewise: かう → かえば, いう → いえば. And remember that ほど in comparisons needs a negative: ふみこさん ほど じょうず じゃ ない.

よなか の あかり — The light in the middle of the night
On the evening before the sisters left, everyone gathered again at Mihai and Ana’s home.
Mrs Doina brought cherry jam she had made herself, Mr Petre brought wine, and Elena brought cozonac.
Last of all came Ioana, with flowers, a little late.
Ioana bowed deeply at the door and said the words she had practised countless times: “Thank you for inviting me today.”
Mrs Fumiko smiled and answered: “The pleasure is mine. Next time, let’s meet in Kyoto.”
Ioana said “yes!”, then quickly corrected herself: “…I will certainly come (to visit you).” Everyone laughed.
That evening, Mrs Doina tried making the tea by herself for the first time.
Looking at Mrs Fumiko’s card, she let the water cool a little and poured a little at a time, in turn.
After one sip, Mrs Fumiko’s eyes went wide: “Mrs Doina, it’s good!”
“Really? It’s still bitter, but the more I drink it, the more I like it.”
Mr Petre said “I’d like to let my dog have some too”, and made everyone laugh again.
Elena asked Mrs Fumiko, through Mihai: “Could I come to your teahouse in Kyoto someday too?”
Mrs Fumiko put her hands together and answered: “Of course. Please do come together with them. I’ll be waiting for you.”
“All the way to Japan to drink bitter tea?” Elena laughed, but her eyes were shining with joy.
In the middle of the night, Ana woke up because the baby in her tummy kicked her.
When she went to get a drink of water, a thin line of light was slipping out from under the door of the baby’s room.
From inside came the soft voices of the sisters.
“Sister, hold it here a little longer.” “Like this? …I wonder if it’ll be ready by tomorrow morning.” “I’ll make sure it is. Absolutely.”
Ana didn’t know what they were doing, but she didn’t knock and quietly went back to bed.
Mihai was fast asleep. Ana smiled in the dark: “What’s secret should stay secret.”
In bed, Ana thought that the sisters fifty years ago had probably whispered just like this, in one room, until late at night.

The next morning, when she opened the box, Ana finally understood. The light of the night before had been the light by which the sisters were sewing a tiny newborn’s garment from their mother’s kimono.
Before Christmas, the airport was full of people.
After check-in, Mrs Fumiko took a small bag out of her handbag. “This is the rest of the hōjicha. Ana, drink a little every day.”
“And please give my regards to your grandfather. I will certainly use that spoon on the day of the anniversary.” “Yes, I’ll certainly tell him.”
Mrs Suzuki gently placed her hand on Ana’s tummy. “Grandma from Madrid will come again soon, you know.” The baby moved, as if answering.
Mihai stood in front of the sisters and bowed deeply. “That you both kindly came here, truly…”
But then his voice caught in his throat. Not a single keigo word would come out anymore.
Mrs Suzuki laughed and patted him on the back. “That’s enough keigo. I’m going back to being the old lady next door in Madrid.”
And, as she had learned in Spain, she hugged Mihai and Ana tightly.
Mrs Fumiko, a little shyly, hugged them both too. “We don’t really do this in Japan… but today is special.”
The people around them turned to look, but the four of them didn’t mind.
The sisters, in their matching scarves, walked off towards the gate holding hands.
They turned around once and waved. They turned around once more and waved again.
“It’s as if they’re holding hands for all fifty years,” Ana said, and Mihai nodded in silence.
In the taxi on the way back, Ana took Mihai’s hand.
“Will we really be able to go, in the spring two years from now? With the baby, so far away.”
“We’ll go. Grandpa said it too: you should see the people you love while you still can.”
Ana nodded and looked out of the window at the white city.
When they got home, the rooms suddenly seemed very quiet.
In the baby’s room were the neatly folded futons and the two thick blankets to give back to Mrs Doina.
On the futon lay a letter from Mrs Suzuki: “Thank you for everything. The nights we slept in this room were like going back to childhood.”
At the end of the letter, in Mrs Fumiko’s handwriting, it said: “We’ll be waiting for you in cherry-blossom season.”
Ana hung the little garment on the wall. On the white fabric, pale pink cherry blossoms are in bloom.
She put the invitation on the shelf, next to the tiny socks and Sakura’s photo.
“This child has been invited to Kyoto even before she’s born.”
Mihai brought the crib, still in its box, out of the storeroom. Now that the futons were gone, there was finally room to assemble it.
“The instructions are only in English and Romanian? I wish they were in Japanese,” Mihai said, and Ana burst out laughing.
In about an hour, the two of them had finished putting the crib together, right under the little garment on the wall.
Ana gently stroked the crib and said: “One more month.”
Towards evening it began to snow outside the window. Ana made some of Mrs Fumiko’s hōjicha and handed Mihai a cup.
“How is it?” “…It’s not as good as Mrs Fumiko’s, but it’s good.” “The more often I make it, the better I get. By the spring two years from now, I’m sure.”
Inside her tummy, the baby gave another little kick. It was as if she were saying: “I’m coming too.”
